text: — Did you hear the news? — cried Marcus Aurelius, as soon as he opened the door and rushed breathlessly into the room.
— What news? — we all called out.
— Bay Ganyo has returned from Europe!
— It can’t be!
— How can it be “impossible,” gentlemen? I saw him, I spoke with him... His first word... ha-ha-ha!... His first word: oples... ha-ha-ha!... We messed it up, say, we did... ha-ha-ha...
— Stop giggling, man — Arpakasha shouted impatiently. — Tell me. Do you want tea?
— Arpakash, let me kiss you between the eyes...
— Cattle! — Arpakash let out with a good-natured smile and handed a cup of tea to Mark Aurelius, while pulling his curly mustache with his free hand. — Chief cattle!
— Captain, don’t spin it, please, steamboat — joked Mark Aurelius, took a sip from the cup, and told us the following:

— Imagine, gentlemen, what happiness: a few days ago, on the 22nd (Alyosha, your favorite number), on Sunday, Gervanich and I went to the Iskar inns, toward Vrazhdebna; we found a whole crowd there...
— Weren’t the Urvich people there?...

— No, they weren’t there; they were at their Urvich... Don’t interrupt me, Arpakash... There was a whole crowd there, mostly foreigners — Germans, Czechs — and not a single one, absolutely not a single one of those apathetic, stone-hearted Shopi... Only old Haji passed by on his way to his estate. The weather, as you know, was wonderful; those meadows, those fields, that fresh green of the forest, you could hardly breathe enough of it... The foreigners had come with their whole families, bringing provisions, bedding, swings for the children; they had settled here and there like bouquets in the shade and were feasting away. It was a pleasure to watch them. And don’t think they were some wealthy, affluent people, no, all of them were common folk, working people — tinsmiths, ironworkers, carpenters. Work six days — feast on the seventh! Not like your honors, sneaking into smoky cafés with your damned “bachka”...
— Marcus Aurelius! Is that you I hear, little dove? John Chrysostom, let me give you a kiss!...
— Be quiet, Arpakash, don’t interrupt me...
— Hey, Amonasro, don’t interrupt the man — Moyshe called out.

— But really, gentlemen — Arpakasha continues his joke with a greasy gaze — tell me, isn’t Marcus Aurelius especially sweet when he pronounces that lovely little word “bachka,” that it’s like an entire piece of music...
— Will you be quiet, Amonasro the Ethiopian?...
— And did you not notice, gentlemen, what bottomless hatred our sweetest Marcus Aurelius bears toward this wench.
— Listen, Amonasro, shut up or I’ll make Moyshe pour a whole glass of cognac down your throat.
— But wha-at clow-ns ours, when they saw the old man in trousers, all of them mocked him and did not give him the girl, taaaa-ra-ra-bum-bie, ta-rara bum...
— You’re crazy, Arpakash, by God, you’re crazy — said Marcus Aurelius with a slight reproach. — Please, be quiet for a moment...
— Enough already, Arpakash! — said Ozhilkata.
— You too, Ozhilka, you too, Brute! Come on, sing “Last night I passed by Sevlievo.”
“Down with Arpakash!” shouted Moyshe, and after him the whole company roared “down!” and finally made the Ethiopian king fall silent.
Marcus Aurelius continued:

— No, indeed, gentlemen, it is a sad phenomenon, this accursed “work,” it has turned us to stone, it has covered our brains with mold and cobwebs. Why, I know some friends who for a whole ten years — ten years! — gentlemen, this is no joke — have not stopped rotting in the smoky corners of the “Panaha” with cards in hand, while before their noses blooms this beautiful, this picturesque city garden, whose breath and coolness they do not know how to enjoy; and outside Sofia, in the surroundings, what wondrous places! We sit in the cafés and sigh for Switzerland, and yet all we need is a little will, and Switzerland, a Bulgarian Switzerland, is before us — Vitosha, Rila, the Rhodopes! The very poorest foreign pauper living in Sofia has enjoyed the magnificent view from Cherni Vrah on Vitosha, and tell me, is there one — one, good heavens! — Shop who has climbed Vitosha! We know examples among the Italian workers who have left ready work here simply because they grow tired of monotony and, at the risk of it, set out wandering to see the world; and on the other hand, there are examples such as, let us say, the shepherd of the Dragalevtsi Monastery, who has spent his whole life looking at the city of Sofia from the heights, has looked at it for years before the Liberation, has watched its destruction, its renewal and expansion, continues to gaze even now, seated in the shade of the walnut tree, at its more splendid appearance, and to this day he has no will to come down from the forest to be curious, to see up close this in every respect interesting transformation of the capital!... But I excuse this peculiar philosopher and even, to tell you the truth, I envy this child of nature! And what shall I say about many of our well-to-do citizens, who choke all their lives in the dust, smells, and miasmas of Sofia’s old streets, look all their lives at the lovely Dragalevtsi grove, and have not had the will to get up, go there, and enjoy its fragrance and coolness, the enchanting murmur of the foaming stream and the nightingales...
— Well, so you’ve turned out to be quite the poet, Marcus Aurelius, just look at you!... But tell me, why are you telling us these old wives’ tales; aren’t you supposedly talking about Bay Ganyo?

— That’s why I’m telling you “old wives’ tales,” because I’m simply angry when I see what kind of apathy has stiffened us... You may say that we do not appreciate natural beauties — no; we cannot help appreciating them, because that is a natural feeling — even cattle appreciate them; but the trouble is that we are paralyzed by Eastern immobility. If I grab you, Arpakash, by the collar and drag you to the Urvich Monastery, as soon as I lead you up behind the Kokalyane hill above the Iskar abyss and you hear the mysterious murmur of the winding foaming river, you will start clicking your tongue and you will exclaim, you will certainly exclaim: “By God, it’s all Switzerland, look, our Bulgaria is beautiful after all, and we fools didn’t know it, while we loaf around in cafés on holidays.” But as soon as you return to Sofia and breathe in its stifling atmosphere, you will fall back into lethargy, apathy will turn you to stone again, until someone else drags you by the collar.

Now — about Bay Ganyo. Gervanich and I spent the whole day wandering through the forest, rolling around on the grass among the trees, eating, drinking, and watching the merry groups of foreigners who had given themselves over body and soul to fun; they had organized various games, sang, ran, jumped — you’d envy them! Toward evening, after a tasty snack, Gervanich and I went into the little inn to drink coffee. After a while, from the direction of the Orkhaniye highway, we heard bells, and shortly afterward, amid a cloud of dust, a carriage with passengers appeared. One passenger got out of the carriage, then a second, and behind the coachman’s back the voice of the third was heard: “Uncle Mihal, take the saddlebags; be careful not to bump them anywhere, so as not to break the flasks, for indeed we have nothing with which to save face before... that one.”

And after those words, out of the carriage jumped... Bay Ganyo. The very same Bay Ganyo, as you know him, before he set out for Europe; with only this difference, that he had put on a necktie and, besides, now had an imposing appearance and a sense of his own dignity and superiority over those around him. The man had been through Europe thick and thin; Europe had become to him like such-and-such... like nothing at all. He tugged at his left mustache, coughed into his hand, and surveyed the semicircle with a glance such as our policemen cast at prisoners, at groups of merry foreigners, and, casting an eye and shaking his head at his ignorant companions, as if he wanted to say to them, “I pity you while you are still alive,” he sighed deeply and meaningfully uttered: “Ah, Prater, Prater!”
— What did you say, your grace? I couldn’t quite catch it — said the man called Bay Mihal.

— May I live to mourn you all — said Bay Ganyo compassionately. — Ah, Prater, Prater!... Has it ever crossed your mind what a thing this Prater is! But how would it ever cross your mind. And if I were to start telling you about it — you wouldn’t be able to understand it.

And in order to show his simple companions, who were capable of understanding him, he approached one of the merry groups, beside which several emptied beer barrels were rolling about, and, with an ironic smile, pointed with his eyes toward the little grove and said: “Das ist bulgarische Prater, ha-ha-ha!…”

The whole group, with eyes cheerfully blurred by the beer, looked our “German” up and down, and one of the company, without paying heed to Bay Ganyo’s ironic remark, handed him a glass of stale wine, saying: — We beg you, sir, would you like beer?
“Even these don’t understand me,” thought Bay Ganyo, and when he returned to his companions, he added: “They got drunk like... Cossacks.”

After that the company entered the tavern and sat down near us. I was with my back to them, and Bay Ganyo could not recognize me; and that he did not recognize me was clear from the words he let slip at our expense: “These too must have got drunk. German goods!”
The servant approached the travelers and began to wipe the table:
— Don’t you want anything? — he asked.
— We don’t want any, we have our own. But, come on, never mind, give us some water and a little fire: pour some fresh water — ordered Bay Ganyo.
Among the passengers, a mysterious serious conversation began, from which not all the words reached us.
— This evening we’ll hardly see the big man; it will be late — whispered Bay Ganyo — we’ll send him the gifts and let him know for tomorrow; then he’ll tell us when to go to the prince.
— And for the prince, something as a gift? — asked old Mihal cautiously.

— No need — answers Bay Ganyo authoritatively, — here everything is about the big shots; if you blind his eyes, you can go off in your white drawers. We’ll give him that thing the lawyer wrote for us, let him read it, and if there’s anything to correct — that’s his business! Behave yourselves before the prince, hey, so no one gets scared. You watch what I do. When I say, as they told us to say: “Your Royal Highness, for heaven’s sake do not accept his resignation, because of the Zadneprian province,” and you after me: “For heaven’s sake, Your Royal Highness!”
— Helbetya, what else shall we say — replies old Mihal humbly.
— Hey, Mihal, you smell a bit like boots, and who knows you? Use your head! — бай Ганьо warns in a fatherly, instructive tone.
— Who? Me? — old Mihal excuses himself. — Don’t say that, brother, someone might hear. Even walls have ears. When I hear the name “Cossack,” I get the shivers.

— Fever’s got you, eh? — whispered Bay Ganyo softly, with a wink. — And when the Russians came, who stole the cattle from the Turkish villages, eh? Since when have you had these riches, eh? Come on, say it!
— But come now, Bay Ganyo, let’s speak frankly — whispers Bay Michal — the mills were left to you from Russian times, weren’t they? Tell me, isn’t that so?
— Come, come, one can’t have a proper conversation with you. It was what it was. Now it’s not like that. Now it’s the Zadneprovskaya Governorate, do you understand?
— Oh, how could I not understand! — said old Mihal and devilishly winked at his companions.
All three laughed into their hands so that no one would hear them.
— Well, use your heads, keep quiet, because if someone hears you—we’re in for a racket... Hey, boy, what’s that newspaper over there? Is it “Svoboda”? — Bay Ganyo turned to the servant.
— “Free speech,” sir.
— Oh, how I’d like to do a little reading — Bay Ganyo whispers to his companions — but I’m afraid, the devil take it. The big shot will hear — and then go sort yourself out afterward.

But just at that moment a scene occurred that made the passengers freeze in their seats. A little boy of five or six was lazily pacing about the threshold of the inn and singing some improvisations, and, apparently under the impression of the three-day-long Sofia incessant “down” in the motif of “Shumi Maritsa,” he abandoned the actual text and, carried away in his song, used the following words, implanted in his brain: “Do-lu-lu, do-lu, do-lu-lu, do-lu, do-o-lu, do-o-lu, do-lu Stambolov!” A hearty laugh from the merry groups interrupted the child’s improvisation, and he, excited by the unexpected success, again, in a louder voice, almost shouting, continued his song and instead of ma-arsh, ma-arsh!—was crying “do-o, do-o, down with Stambolov, do-do-do-doown, down with Stambolov.” This time, besides the hearty laughter, there were also applause and shouts of “bravo,” “down,” “down with the libertine,” “down with the tyrant” from a company of young men returning from a walk.
I turned toward the table of the three travelers.

Bai Ganyo and his companions had turned into statues. With mouths open, with eyes staring motionless, their faces expressed such a sorrowful mixture of fear and astonishment that I had no choice but to regret not having a camera... Bai Ganyo was the first to come to his senses, turned his eyes toward the demonstrators, and immediately shuddered as if struck by an electric current: a mounted police officer was passing along the road and hearing those terrible shouts, and instead of drawing his sabre and, like a whirlwind, with a furious cry, whirling it around the heads of those unheard-of rebels, those black souls, those bandits and traitors, he seemed calm, with a good-natured smile on his face... If a volcano had erupted on Vitosha at that moment, it would hardly have stunned our travelers more than this scene...

— We’ve messed it up, haven’t we! — said Bay Ganyo with a desperate sigh. — Ah, Bay Mihal, do go, please, around the counter and peek into “Svobodno Slovo,” see there if you can understand what this business is...
— Nice work, then why don’t you go? Let me see your courage! — replies old Mihal.

— Hey, how stupid you are! What’s the harm in finally taking a peek; pass by the counter, as if you’re looking at the rakia, whistle like that, and with one eye, just like that, look... so there won’t be any new minis... As if! ...
— Impossible thing... Come to your senses!...
— Well, didn’t you see the policeman?... Ah, wait a minute, bear fear, not me fear — I’ll take a look at the newspaper, and to hell with it!

And Bay Ganyo rose from his seat, whistled “Green Leaf” through his teeth, and, glancing about as if absent-minded, made an eagle-like circle toward the counter; he drew near, seized a bottle of cognac by the neck, and, pretending to read its label, twisted his eyes so far to the right that a man facing him would have seen only the whites of them, and his gaze fell upon the folded newspaper, from which only the title “Free Word” could be seen. He dragged his right hand along and, while intensifying “Green Leaf” to drown out the rustling of the newspaper, opened one part of it and, with his eyes horribly twisted to the right, read: “News from the Palace. Today... was received by His Royal Highness the president-minister and the minister of internal affairs Mr. Dr. K. Stoil...” — Something caught in Bay Ganyo’s throat; he coughed; instantly licked his dried lips and cast a twisted eye farther down and read in large capital letters: “Stambol has fallen...”, and Ganya’s heart sank into his boots, he dropped the bottle of cognac and, in order to smooth over the noise he had made, began coughing loudly... Bay Ganyo turned to his companions and said meaningfully. — It was!
— Good health to you, Bay Ganyo! — said Bay Michal.
— It’s over for her! — added Bay Ganyo, and, approaching the table, whispered quietly to his companions: — Stambolov effendi boklatmush! Stoilov now...
— It can’t be, man, what are you thinking! In the newspaper?...
— Of course!
— Could it be some kind of scam?
— What a trick! — cried out Bay Ganyo in a loud voice, and, gathering all his courage, he thumped on the table and shouted: — Hey, boy, bring here “Svobodno slovo”...
The comrades involuntarily lowered their heads and began to look around timidly.

The boy brought the newspaper and handed it by chance to Bay Michal, but he, as if they had handed him a piece of red-hot iron, drew back his hand and pointed with his eyes toward Bay Ganyo. Bay Ganyo took the newspaper and, of course, turned around to see what there was and what there wasn’t in the tavern, and at last, where would Bay Ganyo get so much courage from! But still, a brave fellow! He unfolded “Svobodno Slovo” and began: “Stamb…”

Bai Ganyo coughed, and his companions coughed even more loudly. Bai Michal squinted at the newspaper to see whether his brave companion was reading correctly, and he made sure there was no mistake... The third companion also bent his head toward the newspaper and read, and... he was seized by a fever, and the world spun around him. How many of his deeds and little deeds, slumbering for years under the prosecutor’s cloth, would those two little words drag out into the light of day...

With murmuring, with whispering, with coughing they pecked through the editorial and, after peering here and there through the newspaper, they finally learned and became convinced that the matter was settled.
— We’ve really messed this up! What now? It’s too late now to ask that his resignation not be accepted. Damn it all. Well, Mihal, why are you silent, say what is to be done? — asks Bay Ganyo.
— Tell me, your grace; I am so stunned, as if someone had struck me on the head with a club — replies uncle Mihal in despair.
— Well, Gunya, why are you keeping quiet? Say a word too. What are we to do now, huh?
— Well, do I know. . . Whatever you say, your grace — muttered Ganyo, crushed in spirit.

— Well, don’t you have any brains, you fool! Am I always the one who has to sort you out? — cries Bay Ganyo, almost in tears from despair. — Never mind, come on, I’ll teach you this time too... Do you know what?

On this matter Bay Ganyo thought for a moment with a frown, scratched himself where it did not itch, coughed once or twice into his hand, reached into the pocket of his frock coat, took out a piece of paper folded in four, and handed it to Bay Gunya.
— Read that thing once more, and then I’ll tell you what we’ll do.
— Well then, why don’t you read it, your grace?
— But, Gunyo, kazdarma beni! You know why I don’t read it; you’re more at ease reading those papish words...

Gunyo unfolded the paper and read roughly the following: “Your Royal Highness! Heavenly thunderbolts have fallen upon our unhappy heads! Our five-century slavery is a pleasant dream compared with the dreadful blow the Northern Enemy is dealing us through the resignation of our — oh! are there words! — most brilliant leader, this Cicero, this Newton of the Bulgarian firmament! O tempora, o mores! ‘No, Your Royal Highness! We still believe in the sound judgment of the valiant Bulgarian people and expect that it will not part with the man who is the embodiment of its aspirations and ideals, of everything honest, noble, chaste, progressive, liberal! We shall not believe that Your Royal Highness will entrust power into the hands of those depraved traitors, those ignorant and uncultured nonentities, who day and night strive to undermine the foundations of our state order and to throw our dear fatherland under the stinking boot of the Cossack.

Your Imperial Highness! Timeo Danaos et dona ferentes! The above resolution was adopted by 11,000 of the most distinguished citizens, and Ganyo Balkanski, Mihal Mihalev, and Gunyo Kilipirchikov were authorized to present it at the feet of Your Imperial Highness. Hooray!

— Hey, what a lousy people we are! — says Bay Ganyo, shaking his head and clicking his tongue. — When it comes to lying, the old gypsies are nothing compared to us. Can it really be that bad? 11,000 of the most prominent citizens! Ha-ha-ha! Take away the thousands, how much is left?
— Eleven people — replies Michal.
— Were there that many?
— Well, that’s all, Bay Ganyo, right is right. Didn’t I go with a policeman to collect them?

— What a lousy people!... Now do you know what? There can be no question of going back. You, Gunyo, are quite a lawyer. Come on, roll up your sleeves, please, and let’s all together knock together another address here, for the new one... No, I have paper. And may they not find out that we came to plead for that handsome fellow, or we’re done for. Especially your business, Gunyo... If another prosecutor comes.
Gunyo coughed a little... — Give me the paper and the pen — he said anxiously. — You watch, I’ll write.
And he began to write: “Your Imperial Highness! Heavenly thunderbolts have rained down upon our unfortunate heads!…”
— Now we have to write it backwards. How should we write it?... Wait... Do you approve it like this: “The heavens opened and showered grace upon our fatherland.”
— It simply comes down to the fatherland — says Bay Ganyo, putting in “our dear fatherland.”
— And I also think that without kindness it’s not worth much — says old Mihal.

— All right, I’ve put in “dear.” Next: “Our five-century slavery is a pleasant dream compared to the ugly blow”... Now the reverse: “Our liberation from our five-century slavery is nothing compared to the brilliant event that shattered the chains of the ugly tyrant.” Do you agree?
— You should have added “spawn of hell” too — says Bay Ganyo. — But never mind, later on.
— ...“which the Northern enemy inflicts upon us through the resignation of our — oh! are there words for it! — most brilliant leader, this Cicero, this Newton of the Bulgarian firmament.”

— Now how are we to turn this?... Wait... Here it is: “And what is owed solely to Your Royal Highness, most gracious father and papa, for having accepted the resignation of this — oh! are there words — most hideous tormentor, this Caligula, this Tamerlane of the Bulgarian firmament.”
— Bravo, Ganyo! — exclaimed Bay Ganyo, his eyes shining with delight.
— How do you mean, Gunya? — Mihal flatters.

— „O tempora, o mores!“... This can stay. It’s one of those things that, wherever you put it, it still fits... „No, Your Imperial Highness!“... Let us put: „Yes, Your Imperial Highness!... We still believe in the sound sense of the valiant Bulgarian people and expect that they will not part with the man...“ Now instead of „will not part with“ we shall put „and will wipe from the face of the earth“, and instead of „the man“ we shall put „the savage beast“.
— No, better put “the furious monster,” — corrects Bay Ganyo.
— I, on the other hand, think we should put “Gehenna of Fire” — said Mihal.
— Ah, what a load you’ve shoved in there! Ha-ha-ha! Why on earth “Gehenna of fire”? Better put “the filthy bloodsucker,” says Gunyo.
— Ha, did you see that now! Bravo! — approves Bay Ganyo.

— ...“who is the embodiment of his aspirations and ideals — of everything honest, noble, chaste, progressive, liberal!” Now let us turn it upside down... “who is the embodiment of the people’s misfortune!... of everything dishonorable, vagabond, depraved, obscurantist, and tyrannical!” Further on: “We shall not believe that Your Royal Highness will entrust power into the hands of those depraved traitors, of those ignorant and uncultured nobodies...” How are we to turn it now?... Wait! It has just occurred to me! Here is how: “Allow us, Your Royal Highness, to consider ourselves fortunate and to express our most boundlessly loyal sentiments, because you have entrusted power into the hands of those noble patriots, of those educated and cultured statesmen... who day and night strive to undermine the foundations of our state order.”
— How so! You’ve made a mistake! — said Bay Ganyo, startled.
— Now we will turn it upside down, so instead of “to undermine” we will put “to strengthen.” “And to throw our dear fatherland under the stinking boot of the Cossack.”

— Come now, let’s see — says Bay Ganyo. — Now’s the real pinch! We don’t know, the devil take it, how the present lot will go about it with Moscow. If one knew they wanted to make peace — easy enough, we could write a whole lot of things: “Tsar liberator; tsar protector; brothers of one womb; the German lousy Jews,” and so on; but we don’t know what wind will blow... Fine: “brother Slavs,” but what if today’s ones are against the Slavs, and then all at once you see... hop! — Bay Ganyo a traitor! No, do you know what? Better let’s throw out that bit there about the “stinking boot”...
— Well, then what shall we put!...

— Sto-oy! Don’t rush! We’ll think it over... You know what? Since we still don’t know what wind is blowing, let’s put it both ways, and let them interpret it however they like. Let’s put it like this... “And let us embrace fraternally both the Russians and the Germans... Phew! May God strike them down!...”
— No, that won’t do at all! What is this “sort of, sort of”? Is that how one speaks before a prince! — declares the lawyerly Gunya.

— Well, how does one speak, eh, you brat! Are you going to teach me! — Bay Ganyo flared up. — Do you know who I am? Do you know that I have traveled all over Europe? I’m not a block of wood like you! Do you know that this Irechek-Mirechek, just like that — they stood there with their mouths open listening to me when I started talking. Englishmen, Americans have shown me respect in Dresden... and you are going to teach me manners?... Do you know that I...
— I know, Bay Ganyo, how could I not know — the startled Gunyo excuses himself.
— Well, if you know, what’s there to it... Anyway, write it there as you know...
— Let us write it like this: “...and to place us, if not above, then at least alongside the great European powers”...
— Well then, I agree — approves Bay Ganyo.
— ...“with the great European powers, by restoring us to the greatness of Asparuh and Krum.”
— I agree. Okay.
— Now, further on: “Your Imperial Highness, Timeo danaos et dona ferentes!” ...Instead of it, it would be best to put: “Vox populi, vox dei.” Do you agree?
— At last, at last, put it on. It’s not quite Bulgarian, but if it has to be, what can we do! — agrees Bay Ganyo.
— ...“The above resolution was adopted by 11 thousand of the most prominent citizens and Ganyo Balkanski was authorized...“ and so on; this can remain intact to the very end.
— Should we leave them with only 11 thousand people, or should we raise it by another one or two thousand for the sake of the newcomers? Should we grease the wheels for them?
— Quite a lot, Bay Ganyo. In our town, even if you gathered every blind and lame person, they’d hardly make 11,000, but come on, never mind, it’s for the sake of courtesy, after all!
— I agree... Well then... instead of Ganyo Balkanski, wouldn’t it be more dignified to put “Mister Ganyo” and the like? So the prince can see that we’re not some lowly sort of people, eh?
— And I will say the same — says Mihal.
— Gentlemen, it’s getting late. Come on, let’s go! — shouted the Turkish cabman from the threshold of the tavern. The passengers set off for Sofia.

The next day, gentlemen, I read in one of the local newspapers that before the great gates there had appeared a deputation from Mr. P., consisting of Ganyo Balkanski and others, to express thanks for the liberation from the tyrannical regime.

Two days later, in that newspaper, I read a telegram from the same city, signed in the name of “thousands” of citizens, in which they informed the grandees that Bay Ganyo and his companions were a self-appointed delegation and that the true народни избраници had already set off for the capital to give thanks...

I knew the hotel where Bay Ganyo was staying, and I headed there. I did not want to express indignation at his base deed, not because any indignation would be too feeble to condemn it; but I wished to make an attempt—to see whether it was possible to make this unhappy creature of circumstance realize the full horror of his action.

On the hotel board I read in which room Bay Ganyo was staying and went up the stairs. I knocked on the door; no one answered. I pressed the handle and the door opened. The room was empty. They had gone. On the table I noticed a scrap of paper on which, in Bay Ganyo’s handwriting, was written: “To the editorial office of the newspaper ‘Free Word.’” The last title was crossed out and replaced with “Freedom.” Further on: “The Secrets of Stambolov” — and this too was crossed out and replaced with “Anarchy.” It was clearly visible that the author of the letter had long hesitated which path to take, because on many lines crossed-out words could be seen, replaced by others with meanings completely opposite to them. For example, where “patriots” was written, it was crossed out, and above it was written “highway robbers at noon” — and this too was crossed out, and again “patriots” was written. The whole letter was crossed out with thick lines drawn by an angry hand, because for the second line there was no ink; the pen was dipped once more into the ink and a doubly thicker line was drawn... Beneath the crossed-out lines stood the following words: “You’ve turned us into monkeys, may the devil take you, you scoundrels...”
